terms.latin: rēs novae, rērum novārum f. pl.
evidence: Cic. Cat. 1.3: novīs rēbus studentem (Lewis & Short, s.v. novus)
terms.comment: Political innovation, overthrow (Lewis & Short): to aim at revolution is novīs rēbus studēre; a revolutionary is rērum novārum cupidus (Cic., Sall.; M-O) or studiōsus. Out of context rēs novae can also be plain news or new things.

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.65: dē commūtātiōnibus rērum pūblicārum
terms.comment: A change in general (of seasons, of fortune); with reī pūblicae or cīvīlis, a change of the state’s form, as from kingship to tyranny (Cic. Rep. 1).

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.69: nōn est enim causa conversiōnis
Cic. Flacc. 94: conversiō et perturbātiō rērum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A turning round: properly the revolving of the heavens, then a political overturn (Lewis & Short).
Late Latin for conversiō, of turning in a circle (Lewis & Short); never of politics in ancient Latin.

phrases.latin: cupiditāte rēgnī adductus novīs rēbus studēbat
phrases.english: led on by desire for the throne, he was eager for revolution

phrases.latin: rērum novārum cupidī, victōrēs praesertim et armātī, vim et manūs adferent
phrases.english: the men hungry for revolution, victorious as they are and armed, will lay violent hands on me

phrases.latin: mīrīque sunt orbēs et quasi circumitūs in rēbus pūblicīs commūtātiōnum et vicissitūdinum
phrases.english: and there are wonderful cycles, a kind of round, of changes and reversals in states

sources: Lewis & Short: novus · Lewis & Short: commutatio · Lewis & Short: conversio · Lewis & Short: revolutio
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. revolutionary.
